title: Explain the forwarding per-hop behavior for QoS

questions.question: How do routers classify traffic for QoS?

correct.explanation: Routers classify traffic for QoS using ACLs (and class-maps) to match packets before marking or queuing.

incorrect.explanation: ASICs forward at wire speed — QoS classification is policy-based via ACLs/class-maps, not generic L2 ASIC tables.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Layer 2 ASICs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for classify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "classify", Access control lists satisfies what this question tests — Layer 2 ASICs does not.

incorrect.explanation: Route tables pick next hops — they do not classify flows into QoS classes.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Route tables points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for classify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "classify", Access control lists satisfies what this question tests — Route tables does not.

incorrect.explanation: Frame filters are not the CCNA answer — IOS QoS classification starts with ACL matches.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Frame filters points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for classify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "classify", Access control lists satisfies what this question tests — Frame filters does not.

answerReview.examTip: QoS classification on routers → ACL/class-map match, then mark (DSCP/CoS) and queue.

questions.question: Which measurement describes the variation of consecutive packet time from source to destination?

correct.explanation: Jitter measures variation in inter-packet delay — critical for voice and video QoS.

incorrect.explanation: Bandwidth is capacity (bits per second) — not the time variation between consecutive packets.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Bandwidth points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for measurement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "measurement", Jitter satisfies what this question tests — Bandwidth does not.

incorrect.explanation: Delay is one-way latency — jitter is the change in delay between packets.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Delay points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for measurement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "measurement", Jitter satisfies what this question tests — Delay does not.

incorrect.explanation: Packet loss is dropped packets — jitter specifically tracks delay inconsistency.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Selecting loss for delay variation metric
incorrect.whatItDoes: Loss points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for measurement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "measurement", Jitter satisfies what this question tests — Loss does not.

answerReview.examTip: Voice/video QoS watch jitter — variation in packet arrival timing.

questions.question: Which is a true statement about the Class of Service field?
choices: The Class of Service field is a layer 3 field.
The Class of Service field is only present in 802.1Q frames.
The Class of Service field is present from end to end of a transmission.
The Class of Service field is 6 bits.

correct.explanation: CoS (3 bits) lives in the 802.1Q tag — it is a Layer 2 marking present only on tagged Ethernet frames.

incorrect.explanation: Layer 3 marking uses IP DSCP/ToS — CoS is the 802.1Q priority field at Layer 2.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Placing CoS at Layer 3 with DSCP
incorrect.whatItDoes: The Class of Service field is a layer 3 field. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: This is a Layer 2 process (statement). The Class of Service field is only present in 802.1Q frames. uses Ethernet addresses — not IP headers.

incorrect.explanation: CoS does not survive end-to-end across an IP cloud unchanged — it is a LAN 802.1Q field remapped at trust boundaries.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing CoS persists end-to-end over WAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: The Class of Service field is present from end to end of a transmission. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", The Class of Service field is only present in 802.1Q frames. satisfies what this question tests — The Class of Service field is present from end to end of a transmission. does not.

incorrect.explanation: CoS is 3 bits (0–7) — DSCP is 6 bits in the IP header.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The Class of Service field is 6 bits. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", The Class of Service field is only present in 802.1Q frames. satisfies what this question tests — The Class of Service field is 6 bits. does not.

questions.question: Identify the measurement of packets discarded due to congestion of queues?

correct.explanation: Packet loss measures frames dropped when queues overflow due to congestion — distinct from delay or jitter.

incorrect.explanation: Bandwidth is capacity (bps) — loss counts discarded packets under congestion.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Bandwidth points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Loss satisfies what this question tests — Bandwidth does not.

incorrect.explanation: Delay is one-way latency — loss is packets dropped from full queues.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Delay points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Loss satisfies what this question tests — Delay does not.

incorrect.explanation: Jitter is variation in delay — not the count of packets discarded.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Jitter points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", Loss satisfies what this question tests — Jitter does not.

answerReview.examTip: QoS metrics: loss = drops; jitter = delay variation; delay = latency.

questions.question: Which DSCP marking has the highest priority?

correct.explanation: EF (46) is Expedited Forwarding — the highest-priority DSCP class for real-time traffic like VoIP.

incorrect.explanation: AF43 is Assured Forwarding class 4, drop probability 3 — lower priority than EF.
incorrect.whatItDoes: DSCP AF 43 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", DSCP EF 46 satisfies what this question tests — DSCP AF 43 does not.

incorrect.explanation: AF11 is low Assured Forwarding — far below EF (46) in priority.
incorrect.whatItDoes: DSCP AF 11 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", DSCP EF 46 satisfies what this question tests — DSCP AF 11 does not.

incorrect.explanation: AF00 (CS0) is best-effort default marking — EF is the premium queue class.
incorrect.whatItDoes: DSCP AF 00 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", DSCP EF 46 satisfies what this question tests — DSCP AF 00 does not.

answerReview.examTip: Voice/real-time marking → EF (46); bulk data → AF classes; default → 0/BE.

questions.question: Identify the recommended maximum delay VoIP traffic should not exceed?

correct.explanation: VoIP one-way delay should stay ≤150 ms on CCNA — beyond that, conversation quality degrades noticeably.

incorrect.explanation: 10 ms is ideal lab latency — CCNA cites 150 ms as the practical maximum for VoIP.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 10 ms gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 150 ms satisfies what this question tests — 10 ms does not.

incorrect.explanation: 90 ms is good but not the exam's stated maximum — CCNA answer is 150 ms.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 90 ms gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 150 ms satisfies what this question tests — 90 ms does not.

incorrect.explanation: 300 ms is too high for acceptable VoIP — the recommended max is 150 ms.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 300 ms gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in identify.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "identify", 150 ms satisfies what this question tests — 300 ms does not.

answerReview.examTip: VoIP delay budget → 150 ms one-way max (also watch jitter and loss).

questions.question: Which QoS queue has priority over all other queues in the scheduler?

correct.explanation: LLQ (Low Latency Queuing) gives a strict-priority queue that always drains before other CBWFQ classes.

incorrect.explanation: CBWFQ provides weighted fair queues — LLQ adds a strict priority queue on top.
incorrect.whatItDoes: CBWFQ points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", LLQ satisfies what this question tests — CBWFQ does not.

incorrect.explanation: FIFO has no priority classes — LLQ explicitly prioritizes delay-sensitive traffic.
incorrect.whatItDoes: FIFO points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", LLQ satisfies what this question tests — FIFO does not.

incorrect.explanation: CIR is a contracted rate metric — not a queuing scheduler with priority.
incorrect.whatItDoes: CIR points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "priority", LLQ satisfies what this question tests — CIR does not.

answerReview.examTip: Strict priority for VoIP → LLQ; weighted sharing among classes → CBWFQ.

questions.question: Which method helps combat queue starvation for QoS queuing?

correct.explanation: Policing drops excess traffic at the rate limit — prevents one class from monopolizing queue capacity (starvation).

incorrect.explanation: LLQ provides strict priority queuing — it helps voice but doesn't police excess to prevent starvation alone.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: LLQ as queue starvation prevention via policing
incorrect.whatItDoes: LLQ points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for starvation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "starvation", Policing satisfies what this question tests — LLQ does not.

incorrect.explanation: CBWFQ fair-queues by class — policing enforces hard rate caps that prevent hogging.
incorrect.whatItDoes: CBWFQ points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for starvation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "starvation", Policing satisfies what this question tests — CBWFQ does not.

incorrect.explanation: FIFO has no fairness mechanism — it worsens starvation risk, not combats it.
incorrect.whatItDoes: FIFO points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for starvation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "starvation", Policing satisfies what this question tests — FIFO does not.

answerReview.examTip: Queue starvation fix: policing/shaping rate limits + LLQ for latency-sensitive traffic.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about shaping of traffic for QoS?
choices: Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay.
Shaping drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss.
Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter.
Shaping slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the speed.

correct.explanation: Shaping buffers excess packets above the CIR — introduces delay to smooth output to the contracted rate.

incorrect.explanation: Dropping excess traffic is policing — shaping queues packets instead.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Shaping drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss. implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay. satisfies what this question tests — Shaping drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Shaping causes consistent delay, not jitter (delay variation) — jitter is variable arrival timing.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay. satisfies what this question tests — Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Shaping delays packets in a queue — it does not actively slow individual packets mid-flight.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Shaping slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the speed. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Shaping holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay. satisfies what this question tests — Shaping slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the speed. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Shaping = buffer + delay to meet rate | Policing = drop excess immediately.

questions.question: Which QoS method uses a round-robin scheduler for packet queuing?

correct.explanation: CBWFQ (Class-Based Weighted Fair Queuing) uses a round-robin scheduler across configured traffic classes.

incorrect.explanation: LLQ adds a strict priority queue — not round-robin across all classes.
incorrect.whatItDoes: LLQ points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for scheduler.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "scheduler", CBWFQ satisfies what this question tests — LLQ does not.

incorrect.explanation: FIFO is first-in-first-out — no weighted round-robin between classes.
incorrect.whatItDoes: FIFO points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for scheduler.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "scheduler", CBWFQ satisfies what this question tests — FIFO does not.

incorrect.explanation: PQ (Priority Queuing) serves high queues first — can starve lower queues, not round-robin.
incorrect.whatItDoes: PQ points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for scheduler.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "scheduler", CBWFQ satisfies what this question tests — PQ does not.

answerReview.examTip: Queuing: FIFO (single queue) | CBWFQ (weighted round-robin) | LLQ (CBWFQ + strict priority).

questions.question: Which statement is correct about policing of traffic for QoS?
choices: Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay.
Policing drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss.
Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter.
Policing slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the bit rate.

correct.explanation: Policing drops packets exceeding the configured rate — enforces a hard traffic ceiling with loss.

incorrect.explanation: Holding packets to cause delay is shaping — policing drops instead of buffering.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Policing drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss. satisfies what this question tests — Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause delay. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Policing causes loss, not jitter — dropped packets don't arrive late, they don't arrive.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Policing drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss. satisfies what this question tests — Policing holds packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to cause jitter. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Slowing packets in-queue is shaping — policing discards over-limit traffic.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Policing slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the bit rate. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", Policing drops packets over the configured bit rate to cause loss. satisfies what this question tests — Policing slows packets in the queue over the configured bit rate to adhere to the bit rate. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Policing = drop at token bucket limit | Shaping = queue/delay to average the rate.

questions.question: Why should QoS policing be implemented?
choices: To maintain a contracted burst rate

correct.explanation: Policing enforces a Committed Information Rate (CIR) — traffic above CIR is dropped or remarked.

incorrect.explanation: LAN policing is possible but the primary exam use is enforcing WAN provider CIR contracts.
incorrect.whatItDoes: To help police LAN applications points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for policing.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "policing", To maintain a contracted CIR satisfies what this question tests — To help police LAN applications does not.

incorrect.explanation: Policing limits sustained rate (CIR), not specifically "WAN apps" — it's rate enforcement anywhere.
incorrect.whatItDoes: To help police WAN applications points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for policing.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "policing", To maintain a contracted CIR satisfies what this question tests — To help police WAN applications does not.

incorrect.explanation: Burst is handled by BC/BE token buckets — policing maintains CIR, not burst rate alone.
incorrect.whatItDoes: To maintain a contracted burst rate points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for policing.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "policing", To maintain a contracted CIR satisfies what this question tests — To maintain a contracted burst rate does not.

answerReview.examTip: Policing terms: CIR = sustained rate | BC = normal burst | BE = excess burst.

questions.question: How do congestion avoidance tools help to prevent tail drop?
choices: When the queue depth is full, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped.
When the queue depth is empty, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped.
When the queue depth is below the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped.
When the queue depth is above the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped.

correct.explanation: WRED randomly drops TCP packets when queue depth exceeds the minimum threshold — signals congestion before tail drop.

incorrect.explanation: Drops occur when the queue is filling (above min threshold), not when full.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: WRED drops only when queue full
incorrect.whatItDoes: When the queue depth is full, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Transport protocol (congestion): When the queue depth is above the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. matches reliability, ports, or connection behavior — When the queue depth is full, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. picks the wrong L4 protocol or port role.

incorrect.explanation: An empty queue needs no congestion avoidance — WRED acts as depth rises.
incorrect.whatItDoes: When the queue depth is empty, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Transport protocol (congestion): When the queue depth is above the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. matches reliability, ports, or connection behavior — When the queue depth is empty, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. picks the wrong L4 protocol or port role.

incorrect.explanation: Below the minimum threshold, no drops occur — drops start above min threshold.
incorrect.whatItDoes: When the queue depth is below the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Transport protocol (congestion): When the queue depth is above the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. matches reliability, ports, or connection behavior — When the queue depth is below the minimum threshold, a percentage of TCP packets are dropped. picks the wrong L4 protocol or port role.

answerReview.examTip: WRED thresholds: below min = no drop | min–max = increasing drop probability | max = tail drop.

questions.question: If a traffic is marked with AF31 and another traffic pattern is marked with AF41, which statement explains the traffic markings?
choices: AF31 marked traffic has a better queue than AF41 marked traffic.
AF41 marked traffic has a better queue than AF31 marked traffic.
Both AF31 and AF41 marked traffic has an equal queue.
During high congestion, AF41 queues will be dropped and AF31 queues won’t.

correct.explanation: In Assured Forwarding, a higher class number (AF4x vs AF3x) gets better drop precedence — AF41 outranks AF31.

incorrect.explanation: AF3x is lower priority than AF4x — the first digit (class) determines queue preference.
incorrect.whatItDoes: AF31 marked traffic has a better queue than AF41 marked traffic. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", AF41 marked traffic has a better queue than AF31 marked traffic. satisfies what this question tests — AF31 marked traffic has a better queue than AF41 marked traffic. does not.

incorrect.explanation: AF3x and AF4x are different classes — AF4x receives preferential treatment.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Both AF31 and AF41 marked traffic has an equal queue. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: CAM learning stores one mapping per arrival (statement): AF41 marked traffic has a better queue than AF31 marked traffic. — not both addresses as table entries.

incorrect.explanation: Under congestion, lower-class (AF3x) traffic is dropped first — AF4x is protected more.
incorrect.whatItDoes: During high congestion, AF41 queues will be dropped and AF31 queues won’t. implies the device should discard the frame instead of forwarding or flooding it.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", AF41 marked traffic has a better queue than AF31 marked traffic. satisfies what this question tests — During high congestion, AF41 queues will be dropped and AF31 queues won’t. does not.

answerReview.examTip: AF format: AFxy — x = class (higher = better queue) | y = drop precedence (lower = less likely drop).
